hypothesis: If whorl breadths along a radius form a geometric progression, then in each shell the log of successive whorl breadths (or radial distances) is linear in whorl number, so a constant-W logarithmic-spiral model fits the landmark-digitised coiling outlines with small residuals and a near-constant whorl expansion rate per shell.
pass_criterion: Using the digitised landmarks and the S_Table_3 hangle output, for at least 90% of the 176 gastropod shells with at least 3 measurable whorls, a linear fit of ln(whorl radial distance or breadth) against whorl index gives R^2 >= 0.98. For those shells, the coefficient of variation of successive-whorl ratios (breadth n+1 / breadth n) within a shell is <= 10%.
fail_criterion: Fewer than 75% of shells reach R^2 >= 0.98 on the ln(breadth) versus whorl index fit, or the median within-shell CV of successive whorl ratios exceeds 20%. Either result refutes the generalisation that gastropod whorl breadths form a geometric progression.
interpretation: Thompson's "breadth of whorl along a radius" is read as the radial distance between successive suture or aperture landmarks measured on a sagittal or apical section, and "geometric progression" as a constant ratio between consecutive whorls, i.e. a constant whorl expansion rate. The modern reading allows for helicospiral shells, whose centreline spirals are conical rather than planar. Collins et al. fit logarithmic helicospirals, so the test uses the radial component. This dataset covers gastropods only. It cannot test the Nautilus ratio of about 3 or the ammonoid part of the claim. A pass supports only the gastropod part, and the nautiloid and ammonoid parts remain untested here. Exact column names must be checked in the CSVs and the zip, because the landing page does not list them.

dataset.name: Data associated with: Going round the twist – An empirical analysis of shell coiling in helicospiral gastropods
dataset.publisher: Dryad (data by Collins, Klapaukh, Crampton, Gazley, Schipper, Maksimenko, Hines)
dataset.why_it_fits: It holds images and .tps landmarks for 176 fossil and modern gastropod shells (25 species), plus specimen metadata and hangle model output (S_Table_1, S_Table_2, S_Table_3 CSVs). The whorl expansion rate and landmark radial distances can be used to test whether whorl breadths are in geometric progression. It covers gastropods only, not Nautilus or ammonoids.
